channel.title: Blog on Kashif Nazir
channel.description: Recent content in Blog on Kashif Nazir

item.title: Worth Building, Then Deleting
item.description: Building a personalised weekend game entirely on a phone showed what AI makes worth creating, even when the infrastructure is meant to be deleted.

item.title: The Harness Matters More Than the Model
item.description: Two recent builds showed me that steering, specs, environments, tools, and verification loops often matter more than paying for a stronger coding model.

item.title: Working with Kiro
item.description: Building Surfdeck with Kiro showed that small tasks, standing context, live hooks, and independent review mattered more than the model itself.

item.title: Your Machine Is the Boundary
item.description: Moving local AI projects onto public URLs turns a laptop's invisible safeguards into explicit decisions about identity, permissions, resilience, and cost.

item.title: Clippy Came Back and Is Less Chatty
item.description: Codex pets bring back Clippy's character without the interruption, turning animated assistants into ambient status lights for long-running agent tasks.

item.title: How Long Will It Still Be Yours?
item.description: Software support, subscriptions and entitlement checks increasingly decide how long the devices we buy remain ours to use.

item.title: Multiple GitHub Accounts on One Mac: Folder-Routed Identity Without SSH Keys
item.description: A three-layer setup routes Git commit identity, HTTPS push credentials, and the GitHub CLI account by repository folder, including in headless shells.

item.title: Why I Stopped Using BJJ Notes and Built My Own
item.description: Building a BJJ training log in Notion with Claude turned two years of scattered notes into a connected system of reads, variations, and outcomes.

item.title: What Decides Whether Technology Gets Used
item.description: Technology adoption depends less on what a tool can do than on exit costs, indirect effects and whether non-users have already chosen not to use it.

item.title: The Words Were Never Hidden
item.description: Decoy Font fooled frontier vision models with a typographic illusion, but ordinary OCR found the message underneath.

item.title: A Week Inside Marker
item.description: A week with Marker showed how a writing tool can help by asking questions, challenging structure, and sometimes refusing to manufacture an answer.

item.title: What the Phone in My Pocket Used to Be
item.description: The technologies that changed everyday life rarely announced themselves, and the phone in my pocket is a reminder to be cautious about predicting how AI will arrive.

item.title: What Actually Moves Between AI Tools
item.description: Trying to move a writing setup from Claude to ChatGPT showed the gap between portable memory, portable code, and portable workflow enforcement.

item.title: Heat Is an Availability Problem
item.description: Heat turns availability into a physical dependency, from an overheating laptop in a London flat to data-centre cooling failures.

item.title: The Tabs I Saved for After the Exam
item.description: Clearing saved tabs after the AWS recert showed how quickly useful technical workarounds age into features, obsolete notes, or stale bets.

item.title: The Same Confident Voice
item.description: A heatwave fan problem showed how AI keeps sounding certain when it cannot check whether its answer works in the real world.

item.title: The Web You'll Never Read
item.description: Machine-only web surfaces turn AI discovery into a trust problem when site owners cannot see what crawlers and agents actually receive.

item.title: The Depth the Recert Can't Test
item.description: AWS recertification keeps testing depth in one vendor while the architecture work that matters has become depth across the joins.

item.title: Three Apps, One Feed
item.description: A disrupted London journey, three travel apps, and the difference between confident presentation and trustworthy source data.

item.title: The Why Leaves With the Person
item.description: Legacy systems and prompt-built systems share the same risk: the output can survive long after the reasoning behind it has disappeared.

item.title: The Hold That Used to Be Free
item.description: Why deferring hardware refreshes no longer feels like a free hold when replacement costs are rising in the background.

item.title: I Think It Does This
item.description: Preparing AI training surfaced the difference between knowing a tool and carrying around assumptions that only survive until you have to explain them.

item.title: Sora Broke My Deprecation Reflex
item.description: Sora's shutdown was a reminder that SaaS deprecation dates do not always behave like enterprise software timelines.

item.title: Automation Keeps Hitting the Same Wall
item.description: Zapier, RPA, and AI agents keep running into the same contract gap between orchestration tools and applications that were not built to be automated cleanly.

item.title: A DR Plan Is a Hypothesis You've Never Tested
item.description: A failed backup story about why disaster recovery plans, fault injection, and restore tests only matter once someone has proved the recovery path works.

item.title: A Week on a Three-Week-Old Keyboard
item.description: A week with Yaps showed where on-device voice typing works, where the real world gets in the way, and how quickly a three-week-old keyboard can improve.

item.title: Back on Windows With Mac Habits
item.description: A week back on an old Windows laptop showed what Windows 11 still gets right, what still gets in the way, and how much macOS muscle memory has started to stick.

item.title: The Service Account Problem Has a New Name
item.description: AI agent identity is being treated as a new governance problem, but most enterprises are still carrying the same unresolved service-account hygiene underneath it.

item.title: What Two AIs Saw in My Study
item.description: Asking ChatGPT and Claude the same vision-led room question showed a difference that benchmarks do not always catch: what each model thinks the answer is for.

item.title: What I Stopped Fighting on the SA Pro Recert
item.description: Moving AWS recert notes from OneNote to Notion, using Claude projects for dense study notes, and where the setup paid off on SA Pro weak spots.

item.title: Better Than What It Replaces
item.description: Self-service, automation, and AI testing only matter when they make the real task faster or easier for the person using them.

item.title: Everyone Wants a Good Handover. Nobody Wants to Write One.
item.description: Good documentation feels like overhead until the day it saves the incident, the handover, or your future self from starting again with no context.

item.title: Microsoft's New Outlook Took Two Years to Get Colour Categories Back
item.description: A small missing calendar rule in new Outlook shows the hidden cost of migrating users before the new client can carry their workflows.

item.title: The Ladder Didn't Break When AI Arrived
item.description: AI is eating some junior work, but the route into architecture had already been narrowed by cloud, specialisation, and the loss of accidental breadth.

item.title: AWS Summit London 2026 — Post-Summit
item.description: The AI Builders Breakfast ended up being the most useful part of the day, and it sharpened the same question I arrived with: where the application layer fits in the AWS Summit conversation.

item.title: AWS Summit London 2026 — Pre-Summit
item.description: I've never been to an AWS Summit before. On Wednesday I'm heading to ExCeL London, and I've already had to make some hard choices about how the day runs.

item.title: Why I Couldn't Containerise My Home Server
item.description: A 2013-era i5 meets Docker, WSL, and the reality that hardware ceilings only show up when you try something new.

item.title: Watching AI Learn to Play Red Light, Green Light
item.description: Trying AI Warehouse's Red Light, Green Light simulator and watching reinforcement learning agents shift from chaos to strategy.

item.title: Pilot to Production: The Gap Nobody Plans For
item.description: Pilots get support, rollouts get a prayer. Why OS migrations and AI tool rollouts fail in the same human ways.

item.title: AI for AWS Certs
item.description: I built two custom GPTs to help study for the AWS AI Practitioner exam. The note-creation one ate more time than it saved. The coaching one was worth keeping.

item.title: The Architecture Unbuilt
item.description: There are a lot of ways to build a personal site. I went with the simplest one. Here's what I considered, what I'm planning to build later, and some stuff about AI agents that I didn't expect to care about.

item.title: Building This Site
item.description: How I built kashifnazir.com in two weeks using Hugo, two AI agents, and zero web development experience.
